Dorset: Where England's Coast Tells Its Story

Dorset's coast is a geological textbook brought to life — 185 million years of Earth's history exposed in cliffs, coves, and beaches. For motorcyclists, it offers rewarding riding through some of England's most photogenic coastal scenery, combined with chocolate-box villages and outstanding food. The Jurassic Coast World Heritage Site is the headline, but there's much more to discover.

The Jurassic Coast

From Lyme Regis to Studland, the coast exposes rocks from the Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous periods. The B3157 from Bridport to Weymouth follows the coast closely, passing Chesil Beach and the Isle of Portland. The road is flowing and scenic, with regular sea views. East of Weymouth, the roads to Lulworth Cove and Durdle Door are essential stops.

Corfe Castle and the Purbeck Hills

Corfe Castle is one of England's most dramatic ruins — a shattered Norman fortress atop a conical hill, guarding the only gap through the Purbeck Ridge. The village beneath the castle is picture-perfect, and the road from Wareham through the gap is a satisfying ride. The Purbeck Hills offer ridge-top roads with views across Poole Harbour.

Must-Visit Coastal Stops

  • Lyme Regis — Fossil capital of Britain, the famous Cobb harbour wall, excellent fish restaurants
  • West Bay — Dramatic sandstone cliffs (Broadchurch filming location), working harbour
  • Lulworth Cove — Perfect natural horseshoe bay, geological wonder
  • Durdle Door — Iconic natural limestone arch, England's most photographed coast
  • Swanage — Victorian seaside town with steam railway and sandy beach
  • Studland Bay — Four miles of golden sand, National Trust heathland
Dorset's coast has the rare quality of being both spectacular and accessible. You can ride to world-class scenery without battling mountain roads or dealing with single-track nightmares.

Inland Dorset

Don't overlook inland Dorset. The Blackmore Vale is Thomas Hardy's Wessex — green farmland dotted with medieval churches and golden-stone villages. Sherborne has a magnificent abbey and castle. Cerne Abbas has the famous giant carved into the hillside. The Dorset Downs offer gentle, flowing B-roads through rolling chalk landscape.

Practical Information

Dorset is accessible from London (2.5 hours via M3/A31), Bristol (2 hours), and Southampton (1 hour). Fuel is available in all towns. The coast roads are busiest in July-August — visit in May-June or September for better conditions. The Sandbanks Ferry connects Studland to Poole, avoiding a 25-mile detour around the harbour. faq.a: The Jurassic Coast is a World Heritage Site running from Lyme Regis to Studland, exposing 185 million years of Earth's history in cliffs, coves and beaches from the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous periods. The B3157 from Bridport to Weymouth follows it closely, passing Chesil Beach and the Isle of Portland, with essential stops at Lulworth Cove and Durdle Door.

faq.q: Should I use the Sandbanks Ferry?
faq.a: Yes. The Sandbanks Ferry connects Studland to Poole and accepts motorcycles, running every few minutes. It avoids a 25-mile detour around Poole Harbour, saving considerable time and linking the Purbeck coast directly to the Poole and Bournemouth conurbation.

faq.q: When is the best time to ride the Dorset coast?
faq.a: The coast roads are busiest in July and August, so visit in May-June or September for better conditions and quieter roads. Dorset is easily reached from London in about 2.5 hours via the M3 and A31, Bristol in two hours and Southampton in one hour.

faq.q: What is there to see inland?
faq.a: Do not overlook inland Dorset. The Blackmore Vale is Thomas Hardy's Wessex, green farmland dotted with medieval churches and golden-stone villages. Sherborne has a magnificent abbey and castle, Cerne Abbas has the famous hillside giant, and the Dorset Downs offer gentle, flowing B-roads through rolling chalk landscape.

faq.q: Where can I get fuel and food?
faq.a: Fuel is available in all towns along the coast. Lyme Regis is renowned for its fish restaurants, and the working harbours at West Bay and Swanage offer fresh seafood. Corfe Castle village and the Purbeck towns provide plenty of pubs and cafes for a mid-ride stop.
